v.why: With tiny Adam steps, a smaller batch multiplies the number of updates within 243 epochs and offsets undertraining.
Large batches give few low-noise updates, so a larger step compensates for the lack of updates.
In a 1-layer net width is the only capacity route, so widening relieves the bottleneck.
Wider layers amplify the per-step change in the output, so a high LR with Adam becomes more unstable as width grows.
Narrow nets have little spare capacity, so stronger L2 adds bias without curbing any overfitting.
When narrow layers are the bottleneck, an extra layer supplies the missing capacity.
Strong L2 controls the overfitting that extra width brings, so the added capacity can be used.
Shallow nets are stable under bigger steps and need them to converge in the epoch budget.
Because the penalty scales inversely with batch size, a smaller batch strengthens an already strong L2 into underfitting.
Narrow nets learn slowly and need many updates, which a larger batch removes.
